sections.section_title: Remaining in Galilee and the Brothers' Challenge
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus remaining in Galilee because the Judean authorities seek to kill him, while his brothers — who do not believe in him — challenge him to go public in Judea, using the language of self-manifestation without understanding that Jesus's self-disclosure operates on the Father's timetable rather than worldly strategy.

sections.section_title: Jesus's Time and the World's Hatred
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus explaining that the world hates him because he testifies that its deeds are evil, directly connecting the world's hostility to its own moral condition rather than to divine predetermination of its response.
sections.relevance: The passage explains why the world rejects Jesus: 'it hates me because I testify of it, that its deeds are evil.' The neutral reading connects this directly to the moral explanation for rejection established in 3:19-21 — people reject the light because their deeds are evil, not because God determined them to reject. The hatred is described as 'structural' in the sense that light inherently threatens those who operate in darkness, but the cause is located in the moral condition of the rejectors (their evil deeds), not in a divine decree. This presents rejection as arising from human moral posture rather than from divine determination of who will accept or reject Jesus.
key_phrases: The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify of it, that its deeds are evil
the light is inherently threatening to those who operate in darkness

sections.section_title: Jesus Goes Up Secretly; the Crowd's Murmuring
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus going to the feast secretly rather than publicly, the crowd's divided murmuring about whether he is a good man or leads people astray, and the suppression of open discussion by fear of the religious authorities.

sections.section_title: Jesus Teaches in the Temple; the Source of His Teaching
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus explaining that his teaching originates from the Father who sent him, and that the test for discerning whether his teaching is from God is volitional — willingness to do God's will produces the capacity to recognize divine teaching.
sections.relevance: John 7:17 is a conventional proof-text for human agency: 'If anyone is willing to do his will, he will know of the teaching, whether it is of God or whether I speak from myself.' The neutral reading strongly supports the agency reading. It states: 'The test is not intellectual but volitional: the one who wills to do God's will — who is disposed toward obedience to God — will be able to recognize whether Jesus's teaching comes from God.' The neutral reading further identifies the inability to recognize Jesus's teaching as God-given as 'diagnostic not of intellectual limitation but of volitional resistance — the unwillingness to do God's will,' connecting this to 5:40 ('You are unwilling to come to me so that you may have life'). This places human willingness as the determining factor in spiritual discernment and, by extension in John's framework, in the belief that leads to life. However, the passage directly addresses the mechanism of recognizing divine teaching rather than salvation outcomes per se, keeping it at LEANS rather than STRONG.
key_phrases: If anyone is willing to do his will, he will know of the teaching, whether it is of God or whether I speak from myself
the inability to recognize Jesus's teaching as God-given is diagnostic not of intellectual limitation but of volitional resistance

sections.section_title: The Sabbath Healing and the Argument from Moses
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus constructing a qal va-homer argument from circumcision on the Sabbath to healing on the Sabbath, demonstrating that his action in chapter 5 was consistent with the Law's own priorities, and calling for righteous judgment based on substance rather than surface appearance.

The neutral reading presents the Jerusalemites debating whether Jesus can be the Christ given that they know his earthly origin, Jesus declaring that his true origin is the Father whom they do not know, the failure of an arrest attempt because 'his hour had not yet come,' and many in the crowd believing on the basis of his signs.

sections.section_title: Going to the One Who Sent Me
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus responding to the arrest attempt by announcing his coming departure to the Father, warning that those who reject him will seek him and not find him, with the authorities' inability to comprehend his words carrying dramatic irony.
sections.relevance: The statement 'You will seek me, and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come' implies that the opportunity for belief can be forfeited through present rejection. The neutral reading connects this to Proverbs 1:28-29: 'They will call upon me, but I will not listen to them; the wicked will seek me but will not find me. For they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD.' The scriptural echo locates the cause of the future inability in present human choices — they 'hated knowledge' and 'did not choose the fear of the LORD.' The neutral reading further distinguishes between disciples and rejectors: for the disciples the separation is temporary, while for those who reject Jesus it is permanent. The permanence of the consequence follows from the human posture of rejection, not from divine predetermination. However, this is primarily a warning about the consequences of rejection rather than a direct statement about who determines salvation outcomes.
key_phrases: You will seek me, and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come
they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus's climactic proclamation at the Feast of Tabernacles as a universal invitation to come and drink living water — identified by the author as the Holy Spirit — with the invitation structured around human recognition of need, active response, and ongoing belief.
sections.relevance: Jesus's cry 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink' is a universal invitation whose structure presupposes genuine human agency at every stage. The neutral reading explicitly notes three features: (1) universality — 'if anyone (ean tis) — not limited to a particular group, tribe, or class'; (2) conditionality — 'the one who must come is the one who is thirsty — who recognizes the need'; (3) required action — 'coming and drinking are required. Recognizing thirst is not enough.' The present imperative 'drink' (pineto) indicates ongoing action — 'keep drinking, continue coming.' The neutral reading further notes that 'the one who believes in me' uses the present participle, presenting believing as 'an ongoing condition, not a completed past event.' The invitation is issued by Jesus as part of his central proclamation at the feast's climax, not as an aside. The universal scope resists restriction to a preselected group, and the structure treats human response as a genuine condition rather than a predetermined outcome. However, the passage does not directly argue against determinism — it presents the invitation and its conditions without addressing whether God determines who will be thirsty or who will respond.
key_phrases: If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink
not limited to a particular group, tribe, or class
the one who believes in me

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the crowd's divided response to Jesus — some identifying him as the Prophet, others as the Christ, others objecting on the basis of his Galilean origin versus the scriptural expectation of a Bethlehem Messiah — resulting in a schisma that the author uses to show how Jesus's presence forces divergent responses.

The neutral reading presents the temple officers returning without arresting Jesus because they were disarmed by his unprecedented speech, the Pharisees dismissing both the officers and the believing crowd as ignorant of the Law and accursed, while the author highlights the irony that the untrained officers recognized what the trained Pharisees refused to see.

The neutral reading presents Nicodemus invoking the Torah's procedural requirement of a fair hearing to challenge the council's rush to judgment, advancing his trajectory from nighttime private inquiry to daytime public (if cautious) defense, while the Pharisees respond with ad hominem contempt and a historically inaccurate claim that no prophet arises from Galilee.
